images.alt: A Sinclair QL home computer, a flat black wedge the size of a keyboard, photographed from the front
images.caption: Announced 12 January 1984, twelve days before the Macintosh, the QL was Clive Sinclair's move to leave the toy market behind.

images.alt: A Sinclair QL computer connected to a monitor and switched on, shown as a complete working system
images.caption: Inside the wedge sat a Motorola 68008 — a 32-bit processor with an eight-bit bus, at a price Sinclair could bear.

images.alt: Overhead view of a Sinclair QL computer showing its full keyboard layout
images.caption: QDOS multitasked pre-emptively out of 48 KB of ROM, at a time when the Macintosh and the IBM PC ran one program at a time.

images.alt: A Sinclair QL Microdrive cartridge, a small tape-loop cartridge about the size of a matchbox
images.caption: Storage came from two built-in Microdrives — a continuous loop of tape, fast for its kind but never reliable enough for work you cared about.

images.alt: Close-up view of the Motorola 68008 processor chip removed from a Sinclair QL circuit board
images.caption: The 68008 gave the QL a 32-bit-class processor for the price of an eight-bit one, the compromise that made the machine possible at £399.
